title: Coherent Coordinate Descent: Reusing Old Gradients as Stable Nudges
one_liner: When you can't compute gradients directly, reuse stale old gradients to stay stable and efficient.
lead: In many real problems — like on-device learning or black-box optimization — you can't compute gradients the normal way. The paper introduces Coherent Coordinate Descent (CoCD), a method that turns old, stale gradients from previous steps into computational assets. Recycling those historical gradients with the right coordination keeps the optimization stable and only needs to ask the model one more time per step.

paras: In normal machine learning training, you compute gradients (the direction and size of weight nudges) by running the model forwards, then backwards through every layer to see which weights matter most. But in many real situations this is impossible: your phone has no memory for the backwards pass, or the model is a black box and you can only ask it 'what is the answer to this input' with no insight into how it works inside.

When you can't compute gradients directly, standard workarounds are broken. You could estimate a gradient by running the model twice — once with a weight slightly higher, once slightly lower — but that costs two queries instead of one, so it is sample-inefficient. Or you could randomize which weights you check, which lowers the cost but makes the gradient estimates noisy and unpredictable, so learning zigzags and fails to converge smoothly.

callout.html: CoCD treats old gradients from earlier steps as a stable, reusable resource instead of garbage.

steps.text: Don't throw away gradient estimates from the last few steps.
Each iteration, pick a different one to adjust based on a stale gradient.
Use a slightly larger finite-difference step (the distance you wiggle the weight).
Counterintuitively, the larger step reduces how choppy the loss surface feels, making descent stable.
Get the same descent direction as a full gradient with one forward pass.

paras: Instead of computing a fresh gradient estimate every step (expensive or noisy), CoCD keeps a rolling window of stale gradient estimates and rotates which one it uses. At step t, it applies an update based on the gradient from step t minus some fixed block size. This is called 'recycling' or 'coordinate cycling'.

hidden.h2: Gradient coherence: a measure of how well old directions still point downhill
hidden.name: Gradient coherence
paras: The paper names a new quantity: gradient coherence. It measures how much an old gradient estimate (from step t minus k) still points in a useful direction at the current step t. If the loss surface is smooth, an old gradient direction is still mostly correct. If the surface is choppy, old gradients quickly become stale junk. Coherence quantifies the angle between the old estimate and what a fresh gradient would be.

The paper proves that when you use old gradients in a coordinated, cyclic pattern — always rotating through the same block of coordinates — the coherence stays high enough to guarantee convergence. This is the main theoretical insight.

heat.caption: Darker: more coherent (old gradient still points downhill). Bright highlights: the main quantities.

reads.html: Gradient coherence is a number between 0 and 1 that tells you how useful an old gradient still is. When you recycle gradients in a structured pattern, coherence stays high and convergence is guaranteed.

The paper defines gradient coherence formally via the inner product of historical and current gradients, scaled by smoothness. The cyclic reuse pattern (Block Cyclic Coordinate Descent with warm starts) preserves coherence above a threshold, enabling convergence proof.

mechanism.h2: Why recycling old gradients with the right pattern keeps you converging
paras: Here is the causal chain. In zeroth-order optimization, you estimate a gradient by perturbing a weight and measuring the change in loss. This estimate is cheap (one query) but stale after one step — the model has been updated, so the estimate no longer describes the current state. The naive approach: keep re-computing fresh estimates (expensive) or add randomness (unstable).

CoCD's move: instead of discarding old estimates, reuse them in a cyclic pattern. At step t, you apply an update based on the gradient estimate from step t minus B (where B is a block size). This works because: (1) if the loss surface has smooth, rolling hills rather than sharp cliffs, the old gradient direction is still roughly correct; (2) the cyclic pattern ensures that you eventually touch every coordinate, so every weight gets updated; (3) the implicit smoothing effect (larger finite-difference step sizes reduce how sensitive the surface is to small changes) means the gradient estimates are even more coherent across steps.

The result is a descent algorithm that only needs one query per step, maintains a stable (coherent) descent direction, and converges provably because the coordinate cycling guarantees progress on every weight.

stages.s: Current weight, block of old gradients
Select which old gradient to use (rotate through the block)
Perturb that weight slightly, measure loss change
Apply update based on old gradient scaled by current step size
New weight, old gradients shift in memory

math.words: new weight equals old weight minus step size times the old gradient, with smoothness scaling
symbols: weight value at step t minus 1
step size at step t (can be scaled by smoothness estimate)
gradient estimate from B steps ago
block size: how many steps back to reuse

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Start: weight = 0.5, old gradients in memory: [0.2 (from 2 steps ago), 0.15 (from 1 step ago)].
Step 1: select first old gradient, g = 0.2. Update: 0.5 - 0.1 * 0.2 = 0.48.
Step 2: select second old gradient, g = 0.15. Update: 0.48 - 0.1 * 0.15 = 0.465.
Step 3: compute new gradient, g_fresh = 0.12. Store it, rotate block. Update: 0.465 - 0.1 * 0.2 = 0.445.
Each step only asked the model once. No randomness. Converges steadily downhill.

math.note: The key is the cyclic pattern: you always pick from a fixed block of old gradients, never the newest, so you only need one fresh query per step.

charts.title: Random subspace (randomized baseline)

items.html: If the loss surface has sharp, unpredictable changes, old gradients become incoherent fast. CoCD relies on smoothness; if the surface is jagged with cliffs, recycling fails.
If you wait too many steps before reusing a gradient, it becomes very stale. Choosing B (block size) is a hyperparameter; wrong choice reduces coherence.

Larger steps help smoothing because they average over a wider region of the surface, but they can also miss fine details if the true loss surface has bumps smaller than your step size. The implicit smoothing benefit works best in a sweet spot where you smooth enough to stay coherent but not so much that you skip over important structure.

When the loss surface is reasonably smooth (true for most neural nets because training dynamics favor gentle slopes over sharp cliffs), block size is tuned to the problem, and step size is set to balance smoothing, CoCD converges faster than standard finite differences with fewer queries because the recycled gradients remain coherent and deterministic progress is more stable than randomized sampling.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple neural network (5-layer MLP on MNIST or a toy dataset). Lock away the backwards pass (only allow forward passes) by removing access to gradient computation, simulating a black-box scenario. Run three optimizers in parallel: (1) standard finite differences (two queries per step), (2) random subspace (one query, random coordinate), and (3) CoCD (one query, cyclic coordinate with a block of old gradients). Train each for 100 steps on the same 1000-sample batch. Record loss and final accuracy after training.
demo.metric_eq: convergence_speed = initial_loss - final_loss; final_accuracy = correct_predictions / total_samples
demo.closing: CoCD should reach the lowest final loss in 100 steps and highest accuracy with only one query per step, visibly outperforming both standard finite-differences (two queries, not one) and random subspace (noisy, zigzagging).
